cases.interviewerQuestion: Since the extension can't share cookies with the main app's domain, walk me through how you designed the bearer-token auth flow—how are tokens issued, refreshed, and revoked without a shared session store?
cases.tonyRaw: I solo-built this piece, so the auth design was mine end to end. Since the extension runs in its own origin and can't ride on the main app's cookie session, I issued bearer tokens the extension stores locally and sends on every request to the backend, with the API layer validating and refreshing them rather than relying on a shared session store. Revocation and refresh logic lived server-side so the extension never had to trust anything beyond "send token, get response" — that kept the extension itself pretty dumb, which was the point given it's a separate trust boundary from the main app.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were drawing the boundary between Liveblocks state and TanStack Query state, were there any pieces of data that felt ambiguous — like they could plausibly live in either layer — and how did you decide where they belonged?
cases.tonyRaw: Yeah, the ambiguous case was anything that felt like "document metadata" — things like document title, tags, or status fields that get edited collaboratively but also need to survive outside the live session and show up in list views elsewhere in the app. The test I used was: does this need sub-second sync while multiple people are looking at the same document, or does it just need to be correct and cached reasonably well? If it was the former, it went into the Liveblocks LiveObject even if it meant some duplication; if it was the latter, I kept it in TanStack Query and treated Liveblocks as a live overlay that would eventually reconcile via invalidation rather than the source of truth. That duplication was a conscious tradeoff — I'd rather have a clear sync boundary than one store trying to do both jobs and getting neither right.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were integrating AI-generated output into ProseMirror's typed node document model, what were the trickiest edge cases that broke your assumptions about how the AI's output would map cleanly onto that schema?
cases.tonyRaw: The biggest issue was that AI output is fundamentally unstructured text/markdown-ish content, while ProseMirror expects a strict typed node tree with specific marks and node types — so any assumption that generated content would map 1:1 onto our schema broke almost immediately. Things like nested formatting, malformed lists, or inline styles the model invented that didn't correspond to any valid mark in our schema would either throw on insertion or silently produce invalid document state. I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on this feature and personally designed the state-management layer that sat between the AI output and the document model, essentially a validation and normalization step that coerced generated content into schema-valid nodes before it ever touched the editor's transaction pipeline. We also had to account for two concurrent editor versions in production, so that normalization layer had to be resilient to schema differences across versions, not just a single fixed target.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing the transcript-chunking logic, how did you decide where to split a long meeting transcript without losing context that a later agent step might need — like a decision made early on that gets referenced an hour later?

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were porting the trade metric computation from the TypeORM-based implementation to the GraphQL architecture, how did you validate that the new calculations matched the old ones exactly for those high-volume trader accounts — what was your process for catching subtle discrepancies?
cases.tonyRaw: I worked on porting our trade metric computation from the TypeORM-based implementation into the new GraphQL API architecture, and the main risk was subtle drift in aggregation logic for accounts with high trade volume — things like rounding order, filtering edge cases, or how partial fills got bucketed. My process was running both implementations against the same account datasets and diffing outputs field-by-field rather than trusting a single aggregate number, since a matching total could still mask offsetting errors underneath. Where discrepancies showed up, I went back to stakeholders to confirm which behavior was actually correct before assuming the old system was the source of truth, since some of those edge cases hadn't been well-defined to begin with.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were tuning that debounce delay over those nine months, what were the actual failure modes you kept running into — was it more about losing edits, fighting race conditions with save requests stacking up, or just users getting annoyed by perceived lag?
cases.tonyRaw: It was mostly the save-request stacking problem, not lost edits — with dirty-state tracking the data itself was safe, but if the delay was too short you'd get overlapping save requests firing while a previous one was still in flight, and I didn't want to build a full request-cancellation/queueing layer if a simpler timing fix could avoid it. So the nine months was really about finding a delay window that batched rapid edits into one request without making saves feel laggy to the user. Perceived lag was a secondary constraint I was tuning against, but the primary failure mode driving iteration was request overlap under fast typing.
